docs.text: Rhema ¶ Rhema is a language for writing mathematics questions. A file describes a kind of question as a grammar: what shapes it may take, how hard it is, what its answer is and how it reads. The rhema compiler checks the file and writes the questions out for WeBWorK. # The smallest useful question: the sum of two numbers. synth value on E synth latex on E start E E -> integer_between ( 10 , 99 ) "+" integer_between ( 10 , 99 ) { value = $1 . value + $3 . value latex = str ( $1 . value ) ++ " + " ++ str ( $3 . value ) } prompt "What is [` {E.latex} `]?" answer E . value $ rhema run first.rhm --count 2 1. What is [`82 + 40`]? answer: 122 2. What is [`83 + 52`]? answer: 135 The question and its answer come from the same tree, so they cannot disagree. Difficulty is a budget the grammar spends exactly, chosen when the questions are generated. Grammars import one another, and a file can describe a whole assignment, which compiles to the same paper every time. Install ¶ opam install rhema This installs the rhema command and a library of grammars for arithmetic, algebra, calculus, limits, series, propositional logic, sets and inequalities, vectors, complex numbers, sequences, linear algebra and eigenvalues, counting and probability, and number theory. Until the package reaches the opam repository: opam pin add rhema https://github.com/Project-RHM/Project-RHM.git#v0.1.1 --subpath generator Where to go next ¶ The tutorial Eight short chapters, from the file above to a complete assignment in WeBWorK. Every example on the site is checked by the compiler on each change to the repository. The rhema command Compiling, checking, running and listing files, and how imported files are found. The name ¶ RHM , the project Rhema belongs to, stands for Reversible Hierarchical Mathesis , with the motto Regula · Hierarchia · Mathesis . Reversible A parser reads text into a tree. RHM runs that direction backwards: it builds the tree first and writes the question from it, so the question and its answer are two readings of one object. The first version did this literally, running the Menhir parser's grammar in reverse; the letters R-H-M are Menhir read backwards without its vowels. Hierarchical Questions are trees of productions. Difficulty is a budget passed down the tree, results are computed back up it, and grammars compose into assignments by import. Mathesis After Leibniz's mathesis universalis , a universal method of reasoning by calculation: here, a method of producing mathematics questions by rule. Rhema (Greek ῥῆμα, that which is said, an utterance ) is the name of the language. Its letters sit inside RHM, and it names what a grammar does: it says a question. Authors ¶ Jingming Zhang, Jiaming Lei, Xiaobo Huang, Jiesen Long and Zhiyuan Li, at Beijing Normal-Hong Kong Baptist University ; see Authors . Rhema is free software under the MIT licence; the source is on GitHub .

docs.text: Changelog ¶ Rhema follows semantic versioning: the language's syntax, the builtin functions' names and arguments, and the rhema command's options are the public interface. A breaking change raises the major version; a deprecation is announced one version before the removal. Unreleased ¶ Six new question types , all built answer first: counting.rhm (arrangements, selections and probabilities, with named questions counting and probability ), number_theory.rhm , series.rhm , limits.rhm , eigen.rhm and inequality.rhm . Each has a test that checks its answers independently. Builtins : factorial , choose , permutations , gcd , lcm , pow_mod and mod_inverse on whole numbers ( rhema_integers.ml , with overflow checks); number_latex , a number in LaTeX with fractions as \frac ; and the rays set_above and set_below , rendered (a, \infty) and (-infinity, a] . A union of sets is written A U B in PG without brackets around its parts. A leaf (a generator, a literal or a terminal) may be read as $n.value without a synth value declaration; anything else on a leaf is refused with a hint to write str($n.value) . Fixed : a polynomial with a negative leading term was printed as a difference, 9 - (5 \cdot x^{2} + 4 \cdot x) ; it is now -5 \cdot x^{2} + 4 \cdot x + 9 . Documentation site ( docs/ , mkdocs.yml ): a home page, an eight-chapter tutorial, the language reference with its grammar in EBNF, the command, the builtin functions (generated from rhema doc ), the library and difficulty budgets. Every example file is checked and run in CI, and the site must build without warnings. Fixed : distinct in a set counted two different named questions built on the same rule as repeats, and could confuse rules of two files at the same line; it now compares the question type and the rule's file too. rhema doc groups functions by value type ( matrix2 with the matrices, differentiate with the formulas, the generators on their own) and points to the website. The set listing no longer prints an empty budget list. CI : GitHub Actions builds the package from a clean export on OCaml 4.14 and 5, Linux and macOS, exactly as opam does, installs it into a prefix and runs the command; a second job builds the whole tree with every suite, the documentation examples and site, and the Python checks. 0.1.1 (2026-10-25) ¶ Packaging only. The classic generator and its PG parser, which need pprint and menhirCST , are built in the development profile only, so the package's tests no longer fail on a machine without them ( dune build -p rhema @runtest ). No change to the language or the command. 0.1.0 (2026-10-24) ¶ The first version with a name. Language : Rhema, files .rhm . Attribute grammars with inherited budgets and synthesized attributes; include ; import "file.rhm" as name with arguments at the boundary; question NAME { ... } blocks; set NAME { ... } declarations with budgets drawn fixed, from a list, or around a mean; pg_context / pg_width per question; {answer ...} blanks. Values : Number, Formula, Polynomial, Equation, Boolean, Matrix, Set, Vector, Complex, with their builtin functions ( rhema doc ). Difficulty : every library grammar spends a cost budget exactly; --set cost=N ; sets fix the mean of a part. Command : rhema FILE.rhm [-o OUT.pg] , check , run , list , doc ; GNU error format and exit codes; -I and RHEMA_PATH ; one assignment is one paper, --student for a student's own. Library : 24 question grammars, 2 grammar libraries, 1 example set file, installed to share/rhema by dune install . The rhema command ¶ rhema FILE.rhm [-o OUT.pg] [options] compile FILE to WeBWorK PG rhema check FILE... check only rhema run FILE [options] show the questions and answers rhema list FILE the questions and sets FILE declares rhema doc [NAME] the builtin functions (or one of them) rhema --version | --help Compiling ¶ rhema FILE.rhm checks the file, generates questions and writes them as a WeBWorK problem file. The output is named after the input ( quiz.rhm gives quiz.pg ), or after the set with --run SET ; -o OUT.pg names it, and -o - writes to standard output. $ rhema calculus.rhm --question integral -o integral.pg $ rhema homework_set.rhm --run homework # homework.pg $ rhema homework_set.rhm --run quick --pg-dir out/ --pg-dir DIR , with --run , also writes one file per question, named question01.pg , question02.pg and so on. Options ¶ --question NAME One of the file's named questions. The default is main , the question the file declares outside any question block. --run SET The set SET declared in the file. A set names its own questions, counts and budgets, so --question , --count and --set do not apply. --count N How many questions to generate, when not running a set. Default 5. --assignment NAME The assignment this paper is. One assignment is one paper: generating it again gives the same questions. The default is the set's name, or FILE:QUESTION . --student ID A paper of this student's own for the assignment, the same every time and different from the other students' and from the assignment's. --set NAME=VALUE Start an inherited attribute of the question at VALUE , usually the difficulty budget: --set cost=6 . -I DIR Also look for imported and included files in DIR . --ast-out FILE , --visualization-out FILE Save the derivation trees as text, or as an interactive HTML page. Finding imported files ¶ A file named in import or include is looked for, in order: beside the file that names it; in each -I directory, in the order given; in each directory of the RHEMA_PATH environment variable (colon-separated); in the installed library, share/rhema beside the command. So import "calculus.rhm" as calc works from any directory once Rhema is installed. When a file cannot be found, the message lists every place that was searched. Messages and exit status ¶ Problems are reported one per line, as file:line:column: error: message , the form editors and terminals recognise. The exit status is 0 when everything succeeded, 1 when a file has problems or a paper could not be generated, and 2 when the command line itself is wrong. Other commands ¶ rhema check FILE... Checks each file and prints OK with what it declares, or its problems. rhema run FILE Generates and prints questions with their answers, instead of writing PG. With --run SET , prints the set part by part, followed by the mean of each budget in each part. rhema list FILE The file's imports, questions (with start symbol and context), budgets and sets. rhema doc [NAME] Lists the builtin functions grouped by value type, or describes one.

docs.text: Difficulty budgets ¶ Every grammar in the library sets its difficulty the same way: a budget, an inherited attribute called cost , that the question spends exactly. Chapter 2 of the tutorial explains the mechanism; this page is about using it. What a budget pays for ¶ A production pays its price and divides the rest between its parts, and a leaf stands only where the rest of the budget buys it. Prices are chosen so that a harder operation costs more: in arithmetic.rhm a sum costs 1 and a quotient 4, and each digit beyond the first costs 1; in calculus.rhm a product costs 3 because it calls for the product rule, and a function of a compound costs 3 more than a function of x because it calls for the chain rule. The price of every grammar is in the library tables . Cost is not length. One budget buys questions of several sizes, so two questions at the same budget may look different and ask for the same amount of work. Grammars whose questions come in a few fixed forms (a dot product, a cross product, a unit vector) give each form a price and offer it only at exactly that budget. Choosing a budget ¶ The default in each file is a middle difficulty. For a single question type: $ rhema run boolean.rhm --set cost=6 # easy $ rhema run boolean.rhm --set cost=10 # medium, the default $ rhema run boolean.rhm --set cost=14 # hard Small budgets buy few different questions. For boolean.rhm , measured on 500 questions at each budget: Budget Distinct questions Answer true 4 34% 52% 6 63% 54% 8 87% 50% 10 97% 53% 14 100% 53% A set drawn at a budget where few questions are distinct will repeat itself, or fail under distinct , so stay above about 6 for this grammar. An assignment's difficulty is a mean ¶ For an assignment, fix the average rather than every question: 3 of calc . derivative ( cost ~ 6 spread 2 low 2 ) draws three budgets around 6 and adjusts them so that their mean is exactly 6: some easier, some harder, at a known level overall. rhema run reports the mean of each part. See chapter 7 of the tutorial. Measuring a grammar ¶ tools/rhema_difficulty.py in the repository measures what each budget buys: $ python3 tools/rhema_difficulty.py report generator/stdlib/boolean.rhm --at 6,10,14 $ python3 tools/rhema_difficulty.py levels generator/stdlib/boolean.rhm report prints, for each budget, the share of distinct questions, the share of the most common answer, the length of the displayed expression and the size of the derivation tree. levels suggests an easy, a medium and a hard budget: easy is the least budget at which at least half the questions are distinct, medium is the default, hard is as far above medium as easy is below. Giving your own grammar a budget ¶ Declare attribute cost = N split , with N a middle difficulty. Give each production a price with cost = -PRICE and a guard when cost >= PRICE ; give each leaf the guard when cost = 0 (or the price of the leaf, if a leaf has one). Make every budget spendable: from the smallest question upwards, every whole number must be the total price of some tree, or a node will receive a budget no production can take. Check with rhema run --set cost=N over a range of N ; a gap shows as no rule for 'E' fits .

docs.text: The language ¶ This page describes Rhema as the compiler implements it, construct by construct. The tutorial introduces the same material in order of use; the grammar at the end summarises the syntax. Files ¶ A Rhema file is a sequence of declarations , in any order, encoded as UTF-8 and named with the extension .rhm . A file does one or more of three things: declares questions : a start symbol, a prompt and an answer, at the top level (the question main ) or in question blocks; declares sets : whole assignments built from questions; provides productions and attributes for other files to include or import . A file with neither questions nor sets is a library : it can be checked, included and imported, but not run. polynomial_core.rhm and matrix_core.rhm in the standard library are libraries. Lexical structure ¶ Comments run from # to the end of the line. Identifiers are a letter or underscore followed by letters, digits and underscores. By convention nonterminals start with a capital letter ( E , Q ) and attributes, randoms and lets do not; the language does not require it. Integers are decimal digits. A minus sign is an operator, except where a declaration takes a signed integer: the value in attribute , starting values in question blocks, and the draws of a set . Strings are written in double quotes and may span lines; the line breaks are part of the string. The only escapes are \" (a quote) and \\ (a backslash). Any other backslash is kept, so LaTeX is written directly: "\cdot" and "\\cdot" are the same string. Keywords are reserved: answer as attribute boolean context copy import include left let nonassoc on precedence prompt question random require right set split start synth weight when width and or not Inside a set block, the words part , of , any , in , spread , low , allowed , distinct , balanced and ordered have a meaning, but they are not reserved and may be used as names elsewhere. Attributes ¶ Inherited attributes ¶ attribute NAME = INTEGER [ copy | split ] declares an attribute whose value travels down the tree. INTEGER is its value at the root of a question, and must not be negative. The distribution says how a node passes it to its children: copy (the default) every child that is a symbol of the grammar receives the node's value; split the node's value is divided between those children, every division into non-negative whole numbers being equally likely. Leaves (generators and quoted words) receive nothing. A child that is a module symbol ( alias.F ) counts as a symbol of the grammar. The starting value can be changed from outside, with --set NAME=VALUE on the command line, an INTEGER in a question block, or a draw in a set . Synthesized attributes ¶ synth NAME synth NAME on SYMBOL declares an attribute whose value travels up the tree, computed at a node from its children. on SYMBOL restricts it to one nonterminal; without it, every nonterminal must compute it. The same name may be declared on several symbols, but not both with and without on . Every production for a symbol must compute every synthesized attribute that symbol carries. A generator leaf carries one attribute, value , the number it drew; a quoted word carries value , its text. Two names are reserved for the start symbol: pg_context , the WeBWorK context of each question, and pg_width , the width of its answer blanks. When the start symbol computes them, they override the file's context and width for that question. Productions ¶ LHS -> SYMBOL ... [ when EXPR ] [ weight INTEGER ] { EQUATION ... } A production says that the nonterminal LHS may be made of the symbols on the right. The braces are required, even when empty. Each symbol on the right is one of: Written Meaning E a nonterminal, if the file has productions for it; otherwise a terminal that stands for its name + - * / % ^ a terminal that stands for the operator "text" a terminal that stands for the text integer_between(1, 9) a generator: a leaf that draws a number (see builtins ) calc.F or calc.F(cost = cost - 1) a nonterminal of an imported module, with starting values for its inherited attributes $1 , $2 , ... refer to these symbols, counting from 1. when EXPR is the production's guard . The production may be chosen only when it is true. It is evaluated before the children exist, so it may use inherited attributes and question-level values, but not $n . weight INTEGER (a positive integer, 1 by default) is the production's relative chance of being chosen among those whose guards hold. Equations ¶ The body holds equations and requirements, separated by line breaks or commas: NAME = EXPR , where NAME is inherited An update , applied before the children are built: the value is added to the attribute. It must not make the budget negative, and a positive constant is refused, because an update spends a budget. cost = -2 spends 2. NAME = EXPR , where NAME is synthesized Computes the attribute, after the children are built. An equation may use an attribute computed earlier in the same body by its bare name. require EXPR A condition checked after the children are built and the equations above it are computed. When it is false, the node is built again. Updates are applied in the order written; equations and requirements are evaluated in the order written. docs.text: A Rhema file is a sequence of declarations , in any order, encoded as UTF-8 and named with the extension .rhm . A file does one or more of three things: declares questions : a start symbol, a prompt and an answer, at the top level (the question main ) or in question blocks; declares sets : whole assignments built from questions; provides productions and attributes for other files to include or import . A file with neither questions nor sets is a library : it can be checked, included and imported, but not run. polynomial_core.rhm and matrix_core.rhm in the standard library are libraries.

docs.text: Comments run from # to the end of the line. Identifiers are a letter or underscore followed by letters, digits and underscores. By convention nonterminals start with a capital letter ( E , Q ) and attributes, randoms and lets do not; the language does not require it. Integers are decimal digits. A minus sign is an operator, except where a declaration takes a signed integer: the value in attribute , starting values in question blocks, and the draws of a set . Strings are written in double quotes and may span lines; the line breaks are part of the string. The only escapes are \" (a quote) and \\ (a backslash). Any other backslash is kept, so LaTeX is written directly: "\cdot" and "\\cdot" are the same string. Keywords are reserved: answer as attribute boolean context copy import include left let nonassoc on precedence prompt question random require right set split start synth weight when width and or not Inside a set block, the words part , of , any , in , spread , low , allowed , distinct , balanced and ordered have a meaning, but they are not reserved and may be used as names elsewhere.

docs.text: attribute NAME = INTEGER [ copy | split ] declares an attribute whose value travels down the tree. INTEGER is its value at the root of a question, and must not be negative. The distribution says how a node passes it to its children: copy (the default) every child that is a symbol of the grammar receives the node's value; split the node's value is divided between those children, every division into non-negative whole numbers being equally likely. Leaves (generators and quoted words) receive nothing. A child that is a module symbol ( alias.F ) counts as a symbol of the grammar. The starting value can be changed from outside, with --set NAME=VALUE on the command line, an INTEGER in a question block, or a draw in a set .

docs.text: Difficulty is a budget ¶ The questions of chapter 1 are all equally hard. This file asks sums, differences and products of any length, and how long they are is decided when the questions are generated. # Sums, differences and products whose difficulty is a budget. attribute cost = 4 split synth value on E synth latex on E precedence 1 left + - precedence 2 left * start E E -> E + E when cost >= 1 weight 3 { cost = - 1 value = $1 . value + $3 . value latex = infix ( $1 , "+" , $3 ) } E -> E - E when cost >= 2 weight 2 { cost = - 2 require $1 . value != $3 . value value = $1 . value - $3 . value latex = infix ( $1 , "-" , $3 ) } E -> E * E when cost >= 3 weight 2 { cost = - 3 value = $1 . value * $3 . value latex = infix ( $1 , " \\ cdot" , $3 ) } E -> integer_between ( 2 , 9 ) when cost = 0 { value = $1 . value latex = str ( $1 . value ) } prompt "What is the value of [` {E.latex} `]?" answer E . value $ rhema run budget.rhm --set cost=2 --count 3 1. What is the value of [`4 + (4 + 6)`]? answer: 14 2. What is the value of [`3 - 4`]? answer: -1 3. What is the value of [`8 + 2 + 3`]? answer: 13 $ rhema run budget.rhm --set cost=8 --count 3 1. What is the value of [`(4 - 6 + (3 + 4)) \cdot (5 + 8)`]? answer: 65 2. What is the value of [`3 + (7 + 7 + (5 + 7) + (4 - 2 + 5))`]? answer: 36 3. What is the value of [`(6 + 2 - (8 + 5)) \cdot (7 + 8)`]? answer: -75 Productions that refer to themselves ¶ E -> E + E says that an E may be two smaller E s with a plus between them. A grammar like this can make expressions of any size; on its own it would never stop. Something has to say how far to go. Inherited attributes ¶ That something is an inherited attribute , declared with attribute : attribute cost = 4 split Synthesized attributes, from chapter 1, travel up the tree: a node computes them from its children. Inherited attributes travel down: a node receives one from its parent before its children exist. cost starts at 4 at the root (or at whatever --set cost=N says) and is handed down. split says how it is handed down. At each production, what is left of the budget is divided between the children that are symbols of the grammar, in every possible way with equal chance. The other choice, copy , gives every child the whole value; it suits settings that are not spent, such as a limit on the number of digits. Spending ¶ Each production says what it costs: E -> E + E when cost >= 1 weight 3 { cost = - 1 ... } cost = -1 takes one from the budget before it is divided between the two E s. So a sum costs 1, a difference 2 and a product 3, and a number costs nothing. Whatever budget the root starts with, the finished question has spent exactly that much: --set cost=2 gives one difference or two sums, never a product. when cost >= 1 is a guard : the production may only be chosen when it holds. A guard can only look at inherited attributes, because the children do not exist yet when the choice is made. The number production says when cost = 0 , so a number appears exactly where the budget has run out. Among the productions whose guards hold, one is chosen at random, in proportion to its weight (1 when not given). The weights here make sums more common than products. Every budget must be spendable ¶ When a node receives a budget that no production can take, generation stops. Remove the sum production and ask for a budget of 1, which only a sum could spend: $ rhema run gap.rhm --set cost=1 gap.rhm: error: no rule for 'E' fits {cost=1} This is not retried, because no amount of retrying could help: the grammar has no way to spend 1. A grammar that spends a budget should be able to spend every whole number from its smallest question upwards. With prices 1, 2 and 3 and a leaf at 0, this one can. The compiler also refuses a recursion that does not spend. Delete the cost = -1 line from the sum production and check the file: $ rhema check loop.rhm loop.rhm:13:1: error: this rule can reach 'E' again without spending any inherited attribute, so a derivation could circle forever; make the loop consume a budget, for example 'cost = -1' Requirements ¶ The difference production says require $1 . value != $3 . value A require is checked after the children are built. When it fails, that subtree is built again with fresh random choices. Here it rules out differences of zero, such as 7 - 7 , which would make a question cheaper than its price. Prefer guards to requirements where you can: a guard prevents a bad choice, a requirement discards one after the work is done. Brackets come from precedence ¶ precedence 1 left + - precedence 2 left * infix($1, "+", $3) writes its operands with brackets only where the precedence table needs them, which is why the questions above read 4 + (4 + 6) and (6 + 2 - (8 + 5)) \cdot (7 + 8) with no extra brackets. The operator's text may differ from its symbol: the product is the symbol * in the grammar and \cdot in the question. Choosing a difficulty ¶ The budget is how a teacher asks for an easier or a harder question of the same kind: $ rhema run budget.rhm --set cost=3 $ rhema run budget.rhm --set cost=12 Every grammar in the library spends a budget called cost in this way, with prices chosen for its subject; the difficulty page lists them. Chapter 7 shows how a whole assignment fixes the average budget of its questions rather than each one. Next: chapter 3 looks at what the attributes can hold besides numbers and text.

docs.text: A first question ¶ Here is a complete Rhema file. Save it as first.rhm . # The smallest useful question: the sum of two numbers. synth value on E synth latex on E start E E -> integer_between ( 10 , 99 ) "+" integer_between ( 10 , 99 ) { value = $1 . value + $3 . value latex = str ( $1 . value ) ++ " + " ++ str ( $3 . value ) } prompt "What is [` {E.latex} `]?" answer E . value Check it, then ask for three questions: $ rhema check first.rhm first.rhm: OK (1 rules; questions: main; sets: none) $ rhema run first.rhm --count 3 1. What is [`82 + 40`]? answer: 122 2. What is [`83 + 52`]? answer: 135 3. What is [`36 + 76`]? answer: 112 Productions ¶ A Rhema file is a grammar. Its rules, called productions , say what a symbol may be made of. This file has one: E -> integer_between ( 10 , 99 ) "+" integer_between ( 10 , 99 ) { ... } Read it as: an E is a number from 10 to 99, a plus sign, and another such number. start E says that a question is an E . To make a question, the compiler starts from E , picks a production for it, and builds whatever the production asks for, which is how a question becomes a tree: E ├── integer_between(10, 99) 82 ├── "+" └── integer_between(10, 99) 40 integer_between(10, 99) is a generator : a leaf that draws a value. A quoted string such as "+" is a leaf that stands for itself. Attributes ¶ A tree on its own is not a question. The braces after a production say what to compute at that node, from its children: value = $1 . value + $3 . value latex = str ( $1 . value ) ++ " + " ++ str ( $3 . value ) $1 is the first symbol on the right of the arrow, $3 the third. Every generator leaf carries its drawn number as value ; str turns a number into text and ++ joins text. So at the E above, value is 122 and latex is 82 + 40 . These are synthesized attributes : computed from the children, on the way back up the tree. Each has to be declared, with the symbol that carries it: synth value on E synth latex on E The compiler checks that every production for E says how to compute both. Leave one out and it will not compile: $ rhema check first.rhm first.rhm:8:1: error: rule 'E' does not say how to compute 'latex'; add 'latex = ...' inside its braces The prompt and the answer ¶ The last two lines turn the finished tree into a question: prompt "What is [` {E.latex} `]?" answer E . value {E.latex} in the prompt is replaced by the latex attribute of the start symbol. The prompt is written in WeBWorK's PGML, so [`...`] marks mathematics. answer names the attribute the student's answer is graded against. This is the point of writing questions this way. The text the student reads and the answer the grader expects are two attributes of one tree, computed from the same drawn numbers, so they cannot drift apart. There is no answer key to keep in step with the questions. What the compiler checks ¶ Before any question is generated, rhema check makes sure that every symbol used has productions or is a leaf, every synthesized attribute is computed by every production that must carry it, the prompt and answer name attributes that exist, every builtin function is called with the right number of arguments. These are checked once, for the file, not for each question drawn. A file that checks will not fail half way through a paper for one of these reasons. Next: the questions above are all equally hard. Chapter 2 gives a grammar a budget, so that one file can ask easy and hard questions of the same kind.

docs.text: Building on the library ¶ Rhema comes with grammars for most of first-year mathematics. A file can use their parts without copying them. This one asks for second derivatives, using the expressions of the library's calculus grammar. # Second derivatives, built on the library's expressions. import "calculus.rhm" as calc attribute cost = 4 copy synth text on M synth answer_value on M start M M -> calc . F ( cost = cost ) { answer_value = differentiate ( differentiate ( $1 . formula , "x" ), "x" ) require not formula_is_zero ( answer_value ) text = "Find the second derivative of [`f(x) = " ++ $1 . latex ++ "`]." } prompt " {M.text} " answer M . answer_value $ rhema run import.rhm --count 3 1. Find the second derivative of [`f(x) = x^{3} - (\ln\left(x\right) - x)`]. answer: Formula(3*2*x--1/x^2) 2. Find the second derivative of [`f(x) = x \cdot \sin\left(x\right)`]. answer: Formula(cos(x)+cos(x)-x*sin(x)) 3. Find the second derivative of [`f(x) = 5 - x - e^{3 \cdot x}`]. answer: Formula(-(exp(3*x)*3*3)) import ¶ import "calculus.rhm" as calc import loads another file as a module : it is checked on its own, and everything it declares is reached through the name after as . In calculus.rhm From this file the nonterminal F calc.F , on the right of a production its randoms and lets calc.NAME in an expression, {calc.NAME} in a prompt its questions calc.derivative , in a set (chapter 7) Nothing in the module can clash with this file. The library's two Boolean grammars both have a start symbol Q , an attribute cost and a random phrasing , drawn differently; imported as bool and laws they sit side by side. The file is looked for beside this one, then in the installed library, so calculus.rhm needs no path. ( The rhema command lists every place searched.) Using an imported symbol ¶ M -> calc . F ( cost = cost ) { answer_value = differentiate ( differentiate ( $1 . formula , "x" ), "x" ) ... } calc.F is expanded with the module's own productions. $1 is that subtree, and its synthesized attributes are read as usual: $1.formula and $1.latex are what calculus.rhm computes at F . The checker knows $1 is a calc.F and checks the names against the module. Write $1.value for $1.latex and it says: $ rhema check import_bad.rhm import_bad.rhm:15:3: error: $1 is calc.F, which does not carry 'value'; it has formula, latex, constant, monomial, constants_used, linear_terms, power Arguments at the boundary ¶ calc.F(cost = cost) sets the module's inherited attribute cost for that subtree. An attribute not named takes the module's own default; calc.F alone would start at calculus.rhm 's attribute cost = 7 . The argument is computed in this file, before the subtree exists, and the module's budget is its own: the module never sees this file's cost , only the value handed to it. That is what lets grammars priced on different scales work together. A derivative of 8 is harder than a proposition of 8, so a file that offers either writes the exchange rate where they meet: M -> calc . F ( cost = cost ) "derivative" { ... } M -> bool . E ( cost = cost + 2 ) "boolean" { ... } When this file's attribute is split , cost = cost hands the module the share a local symbol would have received, so the budget is still spent exactly across the boundary. include, for extending ¶ include "file.rhm" is the older, simpler mechanism: it pastes the other file's declarations into this one, with no prefix. Use it to extend a grammar, adding productions to its symbols or asking its question with a different prompt. Use import to combine grammars. Next: chapter 7 puts questions from several files into one assignment.

docs.text: calc.F(cost = cost) sets the module's inherited attribute cost for that subtree. An arithmetic sequence has first term [`a_1 = -2`] and common difference [`d = 1`]. (a) Find [`a_{12}`]. [___] (b) Find the sum of its first [`12`] terms. The doubled braces matter in LaTeX. a_{12} needs braces around 12 , and n must be filled in between them, so the prompt says a_{{{n}}} : a literal { , then the value of n , then a literal } . Everything else, the productions, attributes, randoms and lets, belongs to the file and is shared by all its questions. Two questions differ only in where they start and how they ask. docs.text: A whole assignment ¶ An assignment is more than questions drawn one at a time. It has parts, a range of difficulty, no two questions alike. A set says all of that in the file, and rhema turns it into one paper. # Week 3: sequences, differentiation and logic, as one assignment. import "questions.rhm" as seq import "calculus.rhm" as calc import "boolean.rhm" as bool set week3 { part "Sequences" 1 of seq . nth 1 of seq . sum part "Differentiation" 3 of calc . derivative ( cost ~ 6 spread 2 low 2 ) 1 of calc . integral ( cost in { 5 , 7 }) part "Logic" 3 of bool . main ( cost in { 8 , 10 , 12 }) distinct balanced ordered } The file has no question of its own. It imports the sequence questions of chapter 5 and two library grammars, and declares a set: $ rhema run assignment.rhm --run week3 week3: 9 questions in 3 parts 1. Sequences 1(a) [seq.nth] An arithmetic sequence has first term [`a_1 = 0`] and common difference [`d = 5`]. Find [`a_{14}`]. [___] answer: 65 1(b) [seq.sum] An arithmetic sequence has first term [`a_1 = -5`] and common difference [`d = -5`]. Find the sum of its first [`14`] terms. [___] answer: -525 2. Differentiation 2(a) [calc.derivative; cost 5] Differentiate the function with respect to x: [`f(x) = x^{5} - \sqrt{6 \cdot x} + x`]. answer: Formula(5*x^4-6/(2*sqrt(6*x))+1) ... budget means: part 1 Sequences: part 2 Differentiation: cost 5.75 over 4 part 3 Logic: cost 10.00 over 3 Entries ¶ 3 of calc . derivative ( cost ~ 6 spread 2 low 2 ) An entry asks for a number of questions of one type: main or a named question of this file, or alias.name from an imported module. In brackets, it says how to start the question's budgets, in one of three ways: cost = 6 Every question of the entry starts at 6. cost in {8, 10, 12} Each question takes one of the values, and the list is used up before any value repeats: three questions get 8, 10 and 12 in some order. cost ~ 6 spread 2 Budgets are drawn around 6, with a spread of about 2, and then adjusted so that their mean is exactly 6. low 2 keeps every budget at 2 or above. allowed {4, 6, 8} restricts the draw to those values, for a grammar whose forms only exist at certain prices; the mean is then as close to 6 as they allow. The last form is how difficulty is meant to be set for an assignment: not "every derivative costs 6", which makes them all alike, but "the derivatives average 6", which gives some easier and some harder, at a known level overall. The listing ends with the mean of each part's budgets to show it. N of any(A, B) draws each of the N questions from the listed types evenly. Parts and numbering ¶ part "Heading" starts a part. Its questions are numbered 1(a) , 1(b) and so on, under the heading. A set without part lines numbers each question on its own: 1 , 2 , 3 . Constraints ¶ distinct No two questions have the same shape: the same productions, in the same places, with only the numbers different. 3 + 4 and 7 + 2 are one shape. Questions of different types are never repeats of each other. balanced No three questions in a row with the same coded answer, for questions answered with true/false or a small code such as 0, 1, 2. ordered Within a part, easier questions first, by total budget. When a constraint cannot be met, such as distinct over more questions than a grammar has shapes, rhema says which question it could not place instead of trying for ever. The same paper every time ¶ The set's name is the assignment's name, and the paper is fixed by it: running week3 today and next month gives the same questions. docs.text: Values and answers ¶ The answer to a differentiation question is a function, not a number. Rhema computes it, symbolically, from the same object the question shows. # The derivative of a x^n + b x. The coefficients are drawn once per question. random a = integer_between ( 2 , 9 ) random n = integer_between ( 2 , 6 ) random b = nonzero_integer_between ( - 9 , 9 ) let x = formula_variable ( "x" ) let f = formula_add ( formula_multiply ( formula_constant ( a ), formula_power ( x , n )), formula_multiply ( formula_constant ( b ), x )) let f_latex = formula_latex ( f ) synth derivative on Q start Q Q -> "derivative" { derivative = differentiate ( f , "x" ) } prompt "Differentiate [`f(x) = {f_latex} `] with respect to [`x`]." answer Q . derivative $ rhema run values.rhm --count 3 1. Differentiate [`f(x) = 5 \cdot x^{3} - 8 \cdot x`] with respect to [`x`]. answer: Formula(5*3*x^2-8) 2. Differentiate [`f(x) = 6 \cdot x^{6} - 8 \cdot x`] with respect to [`x`]. answer: Formula(6*6*x^5-8) 3. Differentiate [`f(x) = 5 \cdot x^{4} + 5 \cdot x`] with respect to [`x`]. answer: Formula(5*4*x^3+5) Values drawn once per question ¶ random a = integer_between ( 2 , 9 ) random n = integer_between ( 2 , 6 ) random b = nonzero_integer_between ( - 9 , 9 ) A random is drawn once for each question, before any tree is built, and has the same value everywhere it is used. Use one when several parts of a question must agree: the coefficients here, or the truth values of p , q and r in a logic question, which must be the same at every occurrence. random NAME = boolean draws true or false; the other draws are the four generators integer(DIGITS) , nonzero_integer(DIGITS) , integer_between(LOW, HIGH) and nonzero_integer_between(LOW, HIGH) , with whole-number literals as arguments. Values computed once per question ¶ let x = formula_variable ( "x" ) let f = formula_add ( formula_multiply ( formula_constant ( a ), formula_power ( x , n )), formula_multiply ( formula_constant ( b ), x )) let f_latex = formula_latex ( f ) A let is computed once per question, from the randoms and the lets above it. It may call any builtin function. {f_latex} in the prompt is replaced by its value, just as {E.latex} was replaced by an attribute. Types of value ¶ f is not text: it is a formula , a value the engine can differentiate, substitute into, compare and write out as LaTeX or for WeBWorK. Every attribute, random and let holds one of these: Value Made by Graded by WeBWorK as Number literals, arithmetic, generators an exact number, or a fraction Text strings, ++ , str , the *_latex functions (not an answer) Truth comparisons, and , or , not , random ... = boolean 1 or 0 Formula formula_* , differentiate a formula, by equivalence Polynomial polynomial_* a formula Equation equation_* not directly: equation_solution_set gives a Set Boolean bool_* a proposition (Boolean context) Matrix matrix_* a matrix (Matrix context) Set set_* an interval or union (Interval context) Vector vector_* a vector (Vector context) Complex complex a complex number (Complex context) The builtin functions are listed by value type. A function given the wrong kind of value stops generation with a message that names both: values.rhm: error: formula_power expected a number but received "Formula(3)" (This is what happens if the exponent is written formula_constant(n) : formula_power takes its exponent as a plain number.) The answer is computed, not typed ¶ Q -> "derivative" { derivative = differentiate ( f , "x" ) } answer Q . derivative The prompt shows f ; the answer is differentiate(f, "x") . Both come from the one value f , so a question cannot be printed with one function and graded against the derivative of another. The answer is not simplified ( 5*3*x^2-8 rather than 15*x^2-8 ), and it does not need to be: WeBWorK compares formulas by evaluating them, so a student who types 15x^2 - 8 is marked right. Q -> "derivative" is a production whose only symbol is a quoted word. It gives the question a tree to hang derivative on; a file needs a start symbol even when everything interesting happens in let s. Next: chapter 4 gives one question several answer blanks.

Differentiate [`f(x) = 5 \cdot x^{3} - 8 \cdot x`] with respect to [`x`]. answer: Formula(5*3*x^2-8) 2. Differentiate [`f(x) = 6 \cdot x^{6} - 8 \cdot x`] with respect to [`x`]. answer: Formula(6*6*x^5-8) 3. Differentiate [`f(x) = 5 \cdot x^{4} + 5 \cdot x`] with respect to [`x`]. answer: Formula(5*4*x^3+5)

docs.text: random a = integer_between ( 2 , 9 ) random n = integer_between ( 2 , 6 ) random b = nonzero_integer_between ( - 9 , 9 ) A random is drawn once for each question, before any tree is built, and has the same value everywhere it is used. Use one when several parts of a question must agree: the coefficients here, or the truth values of p , q and r in a logic question, which must be the same at every occurrence. random NAME = boolean draws true or false; the other draws are the four generators integer(DIGITS) , nonzero_integer(DIGITS) , integer_between(LOW, HIGH) and nonzero_integer_between(LOW, HIGH) , with whole-number literals as arguments.
docs.title: Values drawn once per question

docs.text: let x = formula_variable ( "x" ) let f = formula_add ( formula_multiply ( formula_constant ( a ), formula_power ( x , n )), formula_multiply ( formula_constant ( b ), x )) let f_latex = formula_latex ( f ) A let is computed once per question, from the randoms and the lets above it. It may call any builtin function. {f_latex} in the prompt is replaced by its value, just as {E.latex} was replaced by an attribute.
docs.title: Values computed once per question

docs.text: f is not text: it is a formula , a value the engine can differentiate, substitute into, compare and write out as LaTeX or for WeBWorK. Every attribute, random and let holds one of these: Value Made by Graded by WeBWorK as Number literals, arithmetic, generators an exact number, or a fraction Text strings, ++ , str , the *_latex functions (not an answer) Truth comparisons, and , or , not , random ... = boolean 1 or 0 Formula formula_* , differentiate a formula, by equivalence Polynomial polynomial_* a formula Equation equation_* not directly: equation_solution_set gives a Set Boolean bool_* a proposition (Boolean context) Matrix matrix_* a matrix (Matrix context) Set set_* an interval or union (Interval context) Vector vector_* a vector (Vector context) Complex complex a complex number (Complex context) The builtin functions are listed by value type. A function given the wrong kind of value stops generation with a message that names both: values.rhm: error: formula_power expected a number but received "Formula(3)" (This is what happens if the exponent is written formula_constant(n) : formula_power takes its exponent as a plain number.)
docs.title: Types of value

docs.text: Q -> "derivative" { derivative = differentiate ( f , "x" ) } answer Q . derivative The prompt shows f ; the answer is differentiate(f, "x") . Both come from the one value f , so a question cannot be printed with one function and graded against the derivative of another. The answer is not simplified ( 5*3*x^2-8 rather than 15*x^2-8 ), and it does not need to be: WeBWorK compares formulas by evaluating them, so a student who types 15x^2 - 8 is marked right. Q -> "derivative" is a production whose only symbol is a quoted word. It gives the question a tree to hang derivative on; a file needs a start symbol even when everything interesting happens in let s. Next: chapter 4 gives one question several answer blanks.
docs.title: The answer is computed, not typed

docs.text: Into WeBWorK ¶ rhema compiles a file to a WeBWorK problem file ( .pg ), ready to upload to a course. Compiling ¶ $ rhema assignment.rhm --run week3 writes week3.pg in the current directory. The output is named after the set with --run , otherwise after the input file ( quiz.rhm gives quiz.pg ); -o NAME.pg names it, and -o - prints it. A single question type compiles the same way. --count says how many questions to put in the file: $ rhema values.rhm --count 10 -o derivatives.pg $ rhema questions.rhm --question sum --count 5 -o sums.pg What the file contains ¶ $ rhema assignment.rhm --run week3 -o - | head DOCUMENT(); loadMacros("PGstandard.pl", "MathObjects.pl", "PGML.pl"); Context("Numeric"); BEGIN_PGML Sequences 1(a). An arithmetic sequence has first term [`a_1 = 0`] and common difference [`d = 5`]. Find [`a_{14}`]. [_____]{65} It is ordinary PG: the macros it needs, the context, and the questions in PGML with their answers in the blanks. Questions that need a different context, such as a proposition to rewrite in the Boolean context, are put in their own PGML block with the context switched before it. One paper per assignment ¶ Compiling week3 again gives the same file, today or next term. The paper is fixed by the assignment's name, which is the set's name unless you give another: $ rhema assignment.rhm --run week3 --assignment "MATH2003 HW3" Two assignments with different names are different papers, even from the same file. Nothing about the paper depends on when or where it was compiled. A paper for each student ¶ When every student should have different numbers, name the student: $ rhema assignment.rhm --run week3 --student 2330026211 -o week3_2330026211.pg Each student's paper is fixed in the same way: the same student and assignment always give the same paper, so it can be regenerated for marking or a resit. Most assignments do not need this; one paper for the whole class is the default for a reason. One file per question ¶ $ rhema assignment.rhm --run week3 --pg-dir week3/ writes week3.pg and also week3/question01.pg , question02.pg and so on, for courses that prefer one problem per file. Uploading ¶ In the WeBWorK course: File Manager : open templates , make a folder for the assignment if you like, and upload the .pg files. Homework Sets Editor : create the set, or open an existing one. Library Browser : choose the course's local problems, browse to the uploaded files, and add them to the set. Open a problem as a student to check that it displays and accepts the answer. The files are plain text and can also be copied into the course's templates directory by anyone with access to the server. Before you upload ¶ rhema run shows exactly the questions and answers that will be in the file, so read the paper there first: $ rhema run assignment.rhm --run week3 That is the end of the tutorial. The reference describes the command in full; the library's grammars, under share/rhema where Rhema is installed, are worked examples of everything above.

This page is generated from rhema doc , so it lists exactly what the compiler accepts; calling one with the wrong number of arguments is an error the checker reports. Numbers, text and rendering ¶ Functions on numbers and text, and the two that write operators with the right brackets. Function Arguments str 1 The text of a number or other value. paren 1 Its argument with brackets around it. infix 3 infix($1, "+", $3) : the two children joined by the operator text, bracketed as the precedence table requires. prefix 2 prefix("\neg", $2) : the operator text before the child, bracketed as the precedence table requires. cond 3 cond(c, a, b) : a when c is true, b otherwise. abs 1 The absolute value of a number. min 2 The smaller of two numbers. max 2 The larger of two numbers. bit_and 2 Bitwise and of two whole numbers; with bit_or , a way to track which of several items a subtree has used. bit_or 2 Bitwise or of two whole numbers. bit_xor 2 Bitwise exclusive or of two whole numbers. number_latex 1 A number in LaTeX: a whole number as it is, a fraction as \frac{p}{q} with its sign in front. Generators ¶ Leaves that draw a whole number. They appear on the right of a production, or after random NAME = ; their arguments are whole numbers.
